I cited absorptive capacity, Amgen's 22.8 percent Phase I approval rate, and AstraZeneca's recovery after 2012. Several people asked the obvious follow up: what specifically about internal science improves acquisition outcomes? Cohen and Levinthal's absorptive capacity says a firm can only recognise and integrate external knowledge to the extent it has its own prior related knowledge. That is the theory. But theory does not explain why some companies integrate a $5 billion acquisition in nine months while others are still reconciling data systems two years after close. The answer is more specific than I made it sound. When you acquire a biotech, you inherit their lab notebooks, their assay databases, their molecular libraries, their clinical datasets. All built on different vocabularies, different metadata standards, different naming conventions. A compound your scientists call a BCL-2 inhibitor lives in the acquired system under a different identifier, described in different units, linked to different endpoints. Multiply that across thousands of compounds. Most acquirers solve this with manual reconciliation. Teams spend months mapping one system to another. By the time the data is usable, the scientists who understood its context have left. The tacit knowledge that made the acquisition valuable walks out during the integration period. EY found that 55 percent of healthcare CIOs cite data integration as their most significant M&A challenge. The companies that integrate fast have something specific: a semantic layer. A shared ontology and data model that makes new information machine readable against existing knowledge from the moment it arrives. Not after months of mapping. On acquisition. AstraZeneca published in Cancer Discovery this year that "semantic layers that support integration for model or agent consumption" are foundational infrastructure for AI driven R&D. They went further: "It is the unique data fabric of each organisation that will increasingly define its edge." The moat is not the model. It is the meaning layer underneath. This reframes M&A entirely. It is not just scientific judgment. It is the speed at which new knowledge becomes usable. A semantic layer makes your fifth acquisition faster than your first because the ontology already covers that biology. Each deal compounds rather than creating another silo. Does your organisation have a semantic layer that could absorb a billion dollar acquisition's data in weeks rather than years? If not, you are not slow at integration. You are structurally incapable of making acquisitions compound. And in a market where deal activity rose 79 percent last year, that is not an IT problem. It is a strategic one.** Sarah Clark liked this [View Post](https://www.linkedin.com/posts/danielhickmore_my-last-post-argued-that-internal-rd-is-activity-7483425445833801728-45F0) - **Professor Richard Scolyer, the world-renowned cancer researcher who famously became 'patient zero' by testing an experimental immunotherapy on his own terminal brain tumor, has died at 59. Diagnosed in 2023 with glioblastoma—one of the most aggressive and incurable brain cancers—Scolyer refused to accept the standard palliative timeline. Instead, the pathologist collaborated with his longtime colleague, oncologist Georgina Long, to adapt the revolutionary immunotherapy techniques they had successfully developed to treat advanced melanoma. In a world-first medical trial on himself, Scolyer received experimental immunotherapy prior to surgery to stimulate his immune system while the tumor was still active. By publicly documenting his treatment and journey in real-time, he provided invaluable clinical data that has already paved the way for new clinical trials in the United States and beyond. Though the experimental treatment did not cure his cancer, it dramatically extended Scolyer's life and fundamentally shifted how researchers approach brain tumor therapies. Before his death on June 7, 2026, the 2024 Australian of the Year expressed hope that his final, deeply personal contribution to medicine would give future patients more time and optimism. His selfless legacy is now immortalized not only through his transformation of melanoma from a death sentence into a manageable disease, but through his courageous final act of turning himself into a living laboratory to advance cancer science. source: Craymer, L.
